CUSHMAN & WAKEFIELD | AMERICAS DATA CENTER MARKET OVERVIEW 1 H1 2026 UPDATE AMERICAS DATA CENTER UPDATE – H1 2026 In the previous edition of this report, the Americas data center market was characterized as one of managed growth. Six months later, that description remains accurate, though the factors shaping growth have become significantly more varied from market to market. Power allocation frameworks, transmission constraints, ratepayer protections, infrastructure funding obligations, regulatory requirements and incentive structures are all influencing how growth is managed across the region. While the industry remains in a period of robust expansion, with capacity under construction reaching a record high, the mechanisms directing that growth have become increasingly localized. Rest assured, growth is not slowing down in any broad sense. The region -wide vacancy rate fell to 3.8% despite 7GW of capacity coming online. The under -construction pipeline continued to expand, reaching nearly 38GW with a 91.7% precommitment rate, while the planned pipeline swelled to 285GW. These headline statistics suggest growth remains firmly in acceleration mode, though the market is no longer experiencing the largely unconstrained expansion that prevailed before 2025. Severe power constraints, growing community opposition and a more restrictive regulatory environment have elevated infrastructure readiness, regulatory certainty, and long -term resource planning as critical factors in project advancement. All of this has created an exceptionally nuanced development environment across the Americas. Continued activity in highly constrained and heavily regulated primary markets demonstrates that added complexity does not necessarily drive demand elsewhere. Operators continue pursuing projects in markets such as Virginia, Atlanta, Chicago and Dallas because the advantages these data center ecosystems provide remain difficult to replicate. Network density, hyperscaler concentration, talent pools and established infrastructure continue to create value that outweighs higher costs, longer timelines and more complex development processes. At the same time, the appeal of secondary, tertiary and frontier markets remains strong. Some of the largest pipeline expansions and most ambitious development proposals in the Americas are now occurring in locations that only recently appeared on site selection shortlists. Cheyenne, West Texas, Alberta and Pennsylvania exemplify this trend. According to our 2026 Data Center Development Cost Guide, the planned development pipeline in frontier markets is nearly equal to that of primary markets in estimated CapEx deployment. Many developers are pursuing both strategies, expanding within established ecosystems while securing positions in emerging markets capable of supporting the next generation of hyperscale and AI infrastructure. Ultimately, the Americas data center market is becoming more complex and more geographically diverse than ever before. Going forward, each market will manage growth in a way that best suits its own interests. The Americas now account for 50.3GW of operational capacity, 94.1% of which is in the United States. Construction activity reached a record 37.7GW, with a 91.7% precommitment rate. Ten markets now have more than 1GW of capacity under construction, four of which are in Texas. The largest single data center availability in an operational facility is 15MW, and there are now 28 availabilities larger than 5MW across the region. Occupiers continue to leverage the development pipeline to meet their capacity requirements. While 39 markets are analyzed individually in this report, all remaining markets are grouped into a “rest of” category representing areas with limited activity diversity. Together, these markets account for 7.8GW of capacity under construction and 77.7GW of the planned development pipeline.

CUSHMAN & WAKEFIELD | AMERICAS DATA CENTER MARKET OVERVIEW 7 Source: Cushman & Wakefield Research | * Definition: Key indicators are based on operational Hyperscale Self -Build & Colo data center facilities in the market and excludes Captive & ICT VIRGINIA AMERICAS PRIMARY MARKET MARKET OVERVIEW Virginia has become the embodiment of a managed growth market. Media headlines focused on legislation, lawsuits, community opposition, power constraints, environmental standards and tax policy debates have become common, creating the impression that new data center development is a futile pursuit in the state. However, Virginia’s market fundamentals continue moving in the opposite direction. In the first half of 2026, the state added more than 1GW of operational capacity, expanded its under -construction pipeline by another 1GW, and grew its planned pipeline to more than 39GW. Growth is not slowing in this market; it’s being managed. The underlying message here is remarkably simple: Virginia has evolved beyond a traditional site -selection decision, and developers are no longer paying a premium for access solely to its land, power or incentives. They’re paying for access to the world’s largest concentration of digital infrastructure and all the benefits that come along with it, as the state’s hyperscale ecosystem, network density, cloud on -ramps, internet exchanges and enterprise connectivity create a value proposition that few competing markets can replicate. This helps explain why land acquisition remains high, why developers continue to pay record -setting land prices, and why projects continue advancing under complex development conditions. There is no doubt that the barriers to development are growing, but the value of being located in Virginia is growing as well. This has led to a significantly tight market characterized by little available space and power and lease rates that continue to climb. The barriers are significant, nonetheless. The Digital Gateway project was officially cancelled, Prince William County continues restricting by -right approvals, and Virginia’s data center tax exemption remains in the crosshairs. New generator standards, large - load requirements, and infrastructure review processes are all changing how projects move through the entitlement and development process, ultimately influencing where projects are built, how they’re powered and what approvals they need along the way. What they have not changed is the market’s trajectory, and that trajectory points toward continued expansion within a managed growth framework. CUSHMAN & WAKEFIELD | AMERICAS DATA CENTER MARKET OVERVIEW 9 Source: Cushman & Wakefield Research | * Definition: Key indicators are based on operational Hyperscale Self -Build & Colo data center facilities in the market and excludes Captive & ICT PORTLAND + EASTERN OREGON AMERICAS PRIMARY MARKET MARKET OVERVIEW Portland and Eastern Oregon are becoming early proving ground for a question many power - constrained markets will eventually face: Will data center developers continue investing if they’re required to pay for most of or all the infrastructure needed to support their projects? Through implementation of the POWER Act and related utility reforms, Oregon has increasingly shifted the cost burden of grid expansion away from residential consumers and onto large -load users. While concerns surrounding power delivery remain central to nearly every development discussion, the market’s recent growth suggests developers remain willing to absorb higher costs in exchange for access to this mature hyperscale ecosystem. Recent market activity suggests the answer is “yes.” More than 300MW was commissioned in the first half of 2026, bringing operational inventory to 3.6GW, and the planned development pipeline expanded from 4.1GW to 5.5GW. This growth occurred despite ongoing concerns about power availability and infrastructure delivery timelines. Recent additions to the planned pipeline appeared in familiar places, with Digital Realty and Stack Infrastructure in Hillsboro and AWS in Boardman. Unlike Phoenix, where developers appear increasingly cautious about future power availability, Oregon’s development pipeline continues to expand even as operators assume greater responsibility for funding growth -related infrastructure. The debate surrounding who should pay for future grid expansion has largely been settled in Oregon. New rates established under the POWER Act are shifting a greater share of costs to data centers and crypto facilities, while hyperscaler disputes with utilities continue highlighting the challenges associated with serving large -load users. Operators are also pursuing alternative approaches, including Aligned Data Centers 31MW battery storage project designed to access grid power years ahead of schedule. Although the cost of growth in Oregon is increasing, the underlying message remains clear: Oregon’s long term value proposition remains strong even as the financial requirements to participate in its market continue to rise. CUSHMAN & WAKEFIELD | AMERICAS DATA CENTER MARKET OVERVIEW 11 Source: Cushman & Wakefield Research | * Definition: Key indicators are based on operational Hyperscale Self -Build & Colo data center facilities in the market and excludes Captive & ICT COLUMBUS AMERICAS PRIMARY MARKET MARKET OVERVIEW Columbus remains one of North America’s most active hyperscale data center markets, with the construction pipeline growing from 1.2GW to 2.0GW during the first half of 2026. The planned development pipeline also grew, rising from 9.8GW to 11.3GW during the same period. Precommitment rates were lower in the first half of 2026 than at the end of 2025, with the under - construction precommitment rate easing from 94.1% in the second half of 2025 to 91.9% in the first half of 2026. The planned precommitment rate dropped significantly from 60.2% in the second half of 2025 to 46.2% in the first half of 2026. This decline was primarily driven by the - build - to - suit and wholesale colocation segments rather than hyperscalers . The Columbus market is leading the nation in the deployment of on -site generation, with operators continuing to pursue natural gas -backed power strategies to accelerate delivery timelines and mitigate utility constraints. EdgeConneX’s proposed 430MW generation facility exemplifies this trend and reinforces Ohio’s position as a national test case for large -scale behind - the -meter (BTM) power deployment. While development activity remains robust, regulatory and political scrutiny have become increasingly prominent. A pause on new data center tax exemptions is now in place pending a broader policy review, reflecting a growing statewide debate over incentives, ratepayer protections and community benefits. Local opposition is also intensifying, and debates impacting Columbus are beginning to mirror those in other major U.S. markets, where electricity consumption, environmental impacts and tax exemptions have become central topics. Despite these challenges, Columbus remains a hyperscale -dominated market supported by continued land acquisition activity, infrastructure investments and a strong development pipeline. Major operators continue to deploy capital throughout the region, particularly in New Albany and surrounding communities, while broader investment in the state supports long -term growth potential. Columbus remains firmly positioned as a strategically important hyperscale market, but regulatory oversight and the market’s ability to balance rapid expansion will dictate the pace of future development. CUSHMAN & WAKEFIELD | AMERICAS DATA CENTER MARKET OVERVIEW 13 Source: Cushman & Wakefield Research | * Definition: Key indicators are based on operational Hyperscale Self -Build & Colo data center facilities in the market and excludes Captive & ICT PHOENIX AMERICAS PRIMARY MARKET MARKET OVERVIEW Phoenix remains one of North America’s largest data center markets, but cautious optimism is warranted over the long term. The market added 151MW of operational capacity during the first half of 2026, bringing total inventory to 2.5GW while vacancy rates eased slightly to 2.7%. This isn’t to say that a pullback in hyperscale investment is underway. Rather, concerns surrounding long -term power availability are growing and beginning to influence how developers evaluate future opportunities in the market. The changing composition of Phoenix’s development pipeline is a notable trend that may reflect growing uncertainty surrounding long -term power availability. Total capacity under construction increased from 1.0GW to nearly 1.6GW in the first half of the year, demonstrating that projects continue obtaining approvals and advancing into construction. However, the planned development pipeline remained flat, meaning that the 600MW that began construction was replaced rather than expanded upon. While 600MW is a significant figure, it falls short of the increases recorded in other major markets, such as Dallas (+3.5GW) and Atlanta (+5.5GW). This suggests that developers are continuing to advance projects already in the queue, but fewer appear willing to make additional commitments until greater certainty exists around long -term power availability. As such, power infrastructure remains the defining variable for Phoenix’s next phase of growth. APS and SRP continue advancing generation, storage and natural gas infrastructure investments intended to support rapidly growing demand, while projects such as Prime Data Centers' PHX01 campus, Microsoft's continued expansion in Goodyear and multiple large -scale developments across Maricopa County highlight continued confidence in projects already underway. The market's challenge is no longer attracting demand but ensuring sufficient power can be delivered to support the next wave of development. CUSHMAN & WAKEFIELD | AMERICAS DATA CENTER MARKET OVERVIEW 15 Source: Cushman & Wakefield Research | * Definition: Key indicators are based on operational Hyperscale Self -Build & Colo data center facilities in the market and excludes Captive & ICT ATLANTA AMERICAS PRIMARY MARKET MARKET OVERVIEW Atlanta’s growth story continues to be defined by scale as the market’s transformation into one of North America’s top hyperscale and AI infrastructure markets persists. Demand from cloud providers, enterprise users and AI -driven deployments remains strong, attracting sustained investment from developers, operators and end users. Atlanta continues to benefit from a combination of strong connectivity, business -friendly policies, available land and a utility actively investing to support future growth. This momentum is reflected in all aspects of the market, from operational capacity and availability to the development pipeline. Expansion remains in full effect in Atlanta as the operational market has grown 7% over the past six months, while the under -construction pipeline increased from 1.3GW to 1.7GW, signaling a near doubling of operational capacity in the coming years. This would bring total operational capacity to more than 3.5GW within the next three to five years. Further underscoring the strength of Atlanta’s demand, precommitment rates for under -construction capacity rose from 94% to 99%, while vacancy in operational facilities compressed from 2.9% to 2.3%. Development ambitions also continued to grow, with the planned development pipeline increasing from 13GW in the second half of 2025 to nearly 19GW in the first half of 2026. Against that backdrop, Georgia Power has continued advancing one of the most ambitious utility expansion programs in the country, which includes 10GW of new generation capacity, including new generation assets at Plant Wansley and transmission infrastructure intended to support the rapidly growing data center asset class. Community opposition is becoming increasingly visible at the local level, and several counties have either considered or enacted moratoriums, zoning revisions or additional development requirements. For example, Project Sail in Coweta County was followed by litigation from local residents after gaining approval, and Georgia Power’s Project Wansley Transmission initiative has generated opposition from landowners along the proposed route. Despite this opposition, projects continue to move forward, further highlighting the strength of demand in the Atlanta market. CUSHMAN & WAKEFIELD | AMERICAS DATA CENTER MARKET OVERVIEW 17 Source: Cushman & Wakefield Research | * Definition: Key indicators are based on operational Hyperscale Self -Build & Colo data center facilities in the market and excludes Captive & ICT DALLAS + FORT WORTH AMERICAS PRIMARY MARKET MARKET OVERVIEW The Dallas market remains the largest data center market in Texas, for now, and is the fifth most active development market in the Americas. While legacy market clusters in Dallas proper, Plano, Richardson, Irving and Fort Worth remain active, much of the market’s future growth is increasingly occurring south of Dallas. Areas such as Lancaster, Red Oak and Midlothian have emerged as focal points for large campus -style deployments due to the availability of larger land assemblages, lower population densities than more urban areas of the metroplex and a viable path to power. As a result, the market’s center of gravity continues shifting southward, where larger -scale development is achievable, while smaller development activity remains broadly distributed throughout the market. The size of the operational market continued to expand throughout the first half of 2026, increasing by 7.6% during the period to bring total operational capacity to 1.8GW. The vacancy rate showed little movement, increasing only 7.5 basis points (bps) even though the market saw 130MW of new capacity come online, indicating both the strength of demand in the market and the market’s ability to absorb new capacity as soon as it comes online. Further evidence of this demand can be seen in the development pipeline, where the amount of capacity under construction rose from 1.2GW in the second half of 2025 to 1.7GW in the first half of 2026 while maintaining a precommitment rate of 93.7%. The planned development pipeline also expanded, rising from 11.9GW to 15.4GW over the same period. Power procurement and grid interconnection continue to influence development activity across the Dallas market, and Texas as a whole. Gov. Abbott’s policy directing data centers to fund the full cost of their interconnection infrastructure, coupled with ERCOT’s evolving Batch Zero framework, has elevated the importance of long -term power planning in this market. While select projects have faced localized opposition and, in some cases, legal challenges brought on by organized opposition groups, investment activity remains strong and the market continues to attract significant commitments from operators seeking to expand in the metroplex. However, New York’s recent moratorium on new data center development has shifted developer attention toward New Jersey. While demand remains closely linked across the region, development activity is increasingly concentrated on the New Jersey side of the market. As a result, the region continues to function as a single market from an end -user perspective while becoming two distinct markets from a development perspective. Market fundamentals remained largely unchanged during the first half of 2026, with operational capacity increasing by a marginal 1.2% and vacancy remaining flat at 6.2%. Sentinel Data Center’s South Brunswick project and a portion of CoreWeave’s $1.8 billion Kenilworth project are the only new developments currently under construction, accounting for 63MW of the 113MW active development pipeline. The remaining capacity under construction consists of expansions to existing facilities or campuses, most notably Equinix’s NY3 and NY6 facilities in Secaucus. With just 418MW in the planned development pipeline, a low figure for a market as mature as New York/Northern New Jersey, activity suggests that operators remain committed to growing within the region but are doing so selectively. Given the increasing divergence between New York and New Jersey’s regulatory environments, future growth is expected to continue favoring the New Jersey side of this bifurcated market, with policy differences remaining as the primary cause. New Jersey’s recent policy initiatives have largely focused on ensuring that large -load users contribute to the infrastructure required to support their developments through proposed tariff structures and clean energy obligations. New York, by comparison, has taken a far more restrictive approach through its moratorium and additional proposed legislation targeting ratepayer protections, infrastructure cost recovery, resource consumption reporting and future data center development approvals. In short, developers may face higher costs in New Jersey, but substantially greater uncertainty in New York. This dynamic will not alter where demand originates, but it will increasingly influence where capacity is deployed and further position Northern New Jersey as the preferred destination.
